reason: Parallelodromous is a venation pattern of the leaf blade, and the examples describe parallel veins. Some examples are fragments ('subparallel to margin'), but the pair is sound.
Strap-shaped is a fair reading of 'ligulate' for corona lobes in Apocynaceae. The 'lingulate' spelling is a hyphenation artefact, but the same shape word applies.
The examples describe a 'corrugate zone' of the corolla, not the petal as a whole, and the word is bound to a zone. Rugose on a petal is rare and would need a bearer for the zone.

'Solitary or fascicled' is a count per node (pattern for number per node), not a spatial pattern. Spatial pattern is a generic attribute and the examples do not describe an arrangement of the cladode itself.
A perianth tube can be constricted, for example above the ovary. The examples are annotated correctly, including the negated one.
The ciliate item is a membrane bordering glands, not the secretory tissue. The bearer is wrong and the quality belongs to the membrane or margin.

Widened wings and the distal end of the column are parts of the gynostemium. Plain widths ('ca. 1.5 mm wide') are measurements, not 'increased width'. A rule would need to separate measurements from widening verbs and to assign the part named in the phrase (wings, distal end).
Involucral bracts (phyllaries) can be bristly, and the examples show this.
Sharpness is a generic attribute here. 'Apiculate' is an apex shape, and the examples mostly describe the apex, not the calyptra. The apex shape needs its own term and bearer.

Sinuous fits a margin or a flexuous stigma branch. Examples mix 'flexuous', 'tortuous' and 'sinuous margin', which are different things. A rule would need to map flexuous/tortuous to their own terms and to take the margin as a separate bearer.
The examples are about the suture, veins and beak of the perigynium, not the perigynium itself. The bearer is wrong, and the quality belongs to those sub-parts.
Optical quality is a generic attribute. The examples are colours (brown, pale, hyaline) and should go to colour terms, not this attribute.
The examples give hyaline margin or tip, not the whole beak. A rule would need a margin or tip bearer, and 'white-hyaline' also has a colour part.
Awns can be ciliate, with cilia along the spiral or the lower part. The examples are correct.
The perigynium orifice can be oblique, with 'obliquely cut' as a related phrase. The bearer is the orifice but is acceptable at perigynium level.
The examples are about a base or an apical appendage of the seed, not the seed. The widened part is a sub-part, so the bearer is wrong.
A perigynium beak can be flat, as in 'flat beak' or 'broad, flat, winged beak'.
A whole plant can be male (staminate, in dioecious or monoecious taxa). The examples are correct, though 'monoecious and male' is odd.
Flower nectaries (discs) can be lobed or unlobed, as the examples show.
Optical quality is a generic attribute. The examples are colours or hyaline margins and should go to colour or transparency terms.
Bark can be platy, forming plates or platelike scales, and the examples agree.
Thorns and spines can be flexible. The examples are correct.
Spines radiate from the areole, as the examples show (radial spines, radiating like spokes).
A tree crown can be sparse or dense.
Infrastaminal scales can be oblong. The examples are correct, from one flora only.
The examples are about antrorse trichomes on the sepal, or sepals pointing forward, which is orientation. They are not about the sepal itself being antrorse. Antrorse belongs to the hairs.
Trichomes can be ciliate, though the examples talk about margins. This is acceptable but low in value.
Achenes can be subglobose, and the examples agree.
The generic shape attribute covers different things in the examples (angled, flat, curved). A rule would need to send each to its own value term. The pair holds no extra meaning.
'Inconspicuous' is a size/visibility remark and the examples mix colour and midrib text. The pair has little meaning for a thorn.
Perianth bristles can be present or absent (a key character in Cyperaceae).
The examples are about a tooth (ligule-like appendage) on the sheath being present or absent. The tooth is a separate part, so the sheath is the wrong bearer.
A corolla lip can be notched, but the examples also mention the lamina and apex. Acceptable at lip level.
The fringe applies to the margin of the lip or its lobes, not the lip as a whole. A rule would need to take the margin as the bearer.
Leaf bases can be thickened, as the examples show.
The examples are counts per node (a number-per-node pattern), and a rule would be better than a pair for this. Amount of the cone itself is not meant.
Pollen cones can be ovoid, and ovate/ovoid fits.
Pollen cones can be sessile or stalked.
The examples are about the beak, vittae and ridges being obsolete, which are sub-parts, so the fruit is the wrong bearer. The French example is about the mesocarp.
Inflorescences (heads) can be straw-coloured, and a colour value is meant.
Pappus scales can be subulate.
The examples are sizes and 'unequal' for glands or parts within the tissue, and a tissue has no size in this sense.
The examples are plain width measurements ('up to 8 mm wide'), not widening. Measurements should be handled by the measurement pattern, not by increased width.
A corolla can be bicoloured.
Trichomes can be twisted or contorted.
A floral corona can be funnel-shaped (funnelform), as the examples show.
Filaments can be suberect. Semi-erect is a fair match.
The undulate part is the margin of the corona or its lobes, not the corona itself. A rule would need a margin bearer, and negations ('not undulate') need care.
Stamens are fascicled as a group (stamens in bundles), not individually. The bearer should be the androecium.
A pseudoparaphyllium can be toothed or dentate, as the examples show.
A leaf margin can be serrate, though the examples add distal/basal position. Serration is meaningful at margin level.
Capsules can be lobed, including the French 'lobées'.
Plant latex can be watery or milky, as in the examples.
Turions can be coloured (olive, green, brown). Colour is meant.
Bulbs can be scaly, with scales on the outer surface.
Filaments can be translucent or pellucid.
The spur belongs to the connective, not the whole stamen. 'Spur shaped' means the stamen has the shape of a spur, a wrong reading of 'spurred'. A spur is a part, so it needs a has-part pattern.
A style (or style head) can be pentagonal in section, as the examples show.
A gynostemium (column) can be cylindrical.
A pappus can be broadened at the base or apex, which is widening, so the pair holds.
